title: The oldest Homo sapiens: Jebel Irhoud
dateNote: Flint tools heated in fires date the fossils to 315,000 years ago, give or take 34,000; a tooth gave 286,000, give or take 32,000. The timeline starts at 300,000 years ago, so the stop sits there.
blurb: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, excavators found skulls, jaws and teeth of early humans lying with stone tools. Flint tools that had been heated in fires date them to about 315,000 years ago. Their faces and teeth look much like ours, but the braincase keeps an older, more primitive shape. They are the oldest fossils yet assigned to our species, Homo sapiens.

title: New tools, and stone from far away
dateNote: Argon and uranium-series dates put the earliest Middle Stone Age layers at Olorgesailie between about 320,000 and 295,000 years ago. The timeline starts at 300,000 years ago, so the stop sits there.
blurb: In the Olorgesailie basin of southern Kenya, people made large hand axes for hundreds of thousands of years. By about 320,000 years ago they were making smaller, carefully shaped points instead, the start of what archaeologists call the Middle Stone Age. The basin has no obsidian, a volcanic glass, yet tools there were made from obsidian found 25 to about 90 kilometres away.

title: Not the only humans
dateNote: Each species has its own dates. The map shows the world about 275,000 years ago.
blurb: Homo sapiens shared the world with other kinds of human. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans further east. In South Africa the small-brained Homo naledi lived between about 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, and the Broken Hill skull from Zambia, of a different lineage, is about 299,000 years old. On Java, Homo erectus lasted until about 110,000 years ago.

title: Many cradles across Africa
dateNote: Florisbad is dated to about 260,000 years ago. For Omo I, 233,000 years ago is a minimum age: the fossil lies below a volcanic ash of that age.
blurb: Jebel Irhoud lies in the far northwest of Africa, but other early fossils with some features like ours come from the south and east. A skull from Florisbad in South Africa is about 260,000 years old, and the Omo I skull from Ethiopia is at least 233,000. Many researchers now think our species took shape across the continent, among groups that split, met and mixed over a long time.
debate: Scerri and colleagues argue that our species formed among many linked populations across Africa, against the older view of one population in one region; the few fossils cannot yet settle it.

title: Early ventures out of Africa
dateNote: Misliya is dated to 194,000 to 177,000 years ago, a date that is disputed. Skhul and Qafzeh fall roughly between 130,000 and 90,000 years ago.
blurb: People of our species left Africa long before the migration that gave rise to most people outside Africa today. A jaw with teeth from Misliya Cave in Israel has been dated to between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago. Burials at Skhul and Qafzeh, also in Israel, date to roughly 130,000 to 90,000 years ago. Ancient DNA suggests an early African group even mixed with Neanderthals.
debate: Sharp and Paces argue that the uranium-series data give the Misliya jaw a minimum age of only about 60,000 to 70,000 years; the excavators defend the older date.

title: Living by the sea
dateNote: The shellfish layers at Pinnacle Point are dated to about 164,000 years ago, give or take 12,000.
blurb: In a cave at Pinnacle Point on the south coast of South Africa, people were eating shellfish by about 164,000 years ago, the oldest known use of food from the sea. Much of Africa was then cold and dry. The same layers hold red pigment that had been worked, tiny blade tools, and stone that had been heated so it would flake more easily.

title: Beads, ochre and the first patterns
dateNote: The Bizmoune beads are at least 142,000 years old; the Blombos finds range from about 100,000 to 73,000 years ago.
blurb: Some of the oldest known ornaments are small sea-snail shells, pierced and worn as beads. At Bizmoune Cave in Morocco they are at least 142,000 years old. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people mixed a red ochre paste in abalone shells 100,000 years ago, engraved lines on lumps of ochre, and about 73,000 years ago drew crossed lines on a stone flake.

title: When did language begin?
dateNote: No date can be fixed. 135,000 years ago is one recent estimate of the latest time by which the capacity for language existed; others put it far earlier.
blurb: Speech leaves no fossils, so nobody knows when language began. Every human population today has full language, so the capacity probably existed before the oldest splits between living populations, which genetic studies place about 135,000 years ago. Some researchers argue that Neanderthals could speak too, which would push language back half a million years or more. The evidence does not yet decide it.
debate: Miyagawa and colleagues argue the capacity for language existed by 135,000 years ago at the latest; Dediu and Levinson argue that it goes back to the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans, more than half a million years ago.

title: When the Sahara turned green
dateNote: Green Sahara periods came and went many times. This stop shows the one around 125,000 years ago, in the last warm interglacial.
blurb: The Sahara has not always been a desert. Changes in Earth's orbit strengthen the African monsoon from time to time, and in the last eight million years the Sahara turned green more than 230 times. Each green phase lasted several thousand years. About 125,000 years ago, green corridors crossed it, possible paths north for animals and perhaps for people.

title: Fire and cooking
dateNote: Burning in Wonderwerk Cave is about a million years old; the cooked starchy plants at Klasies River are about 120,000 years old.
blurb: Our species inherited fire from older humans. Burnt bone and plant ash show fires inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa about a million years ago, and pyrite found with burnt flint at Barnham in England suggests fire was being made there 400,000 years ago. Early Homo sapiens heated stone to make it flake better, and cooked starchy plants in hearths at Klasies River 120,000 years ago.

title: The oldest known burial in Africa
dateNote: The burial is dated to 78,300 years ago, give or take 4,100.
blurb: About 78,000 years ago, in the cave of Panga ya Saidi near the coast of Kenya, a child of two and a half to three years was laid in a dug pit with legs drawn up, and covered with earth. The bones were still joined, so the body decayed where it was placed. It is the oldest known human burial in Africa, though burials at Skhul and Qafzeh are older.
debate: Berger and colleagues argue that Homo naledi buried its dead in Rising Star Cave more than 236,000 years ago; Martinón-Torres and colleagues reply that natural causes have not been ruled out.

title: The Toba eruption
dateNote: The eruption is dated to about 74,000 years ago.
blurb: About 74,000 years ago the Toba volcano on Sumatra erupted, the most explosive eruption of the last 2.6 million years. Its ash fell across the Indian Ocean and as far as South Africa. One theory held that the cold that followed nearly wiped out our species. Yet at sites in India and South Africa, people went on living and making tools above and below the ash.
debate: Ambrose proposed that Toba's volcanic winter caused a human population bottleneck; ash in Lake Malawi shows no major cooling in East Africa, and sites in India and South Africa show people living through it.
